title: Comparison of different reporting methods in different diseases with conductive hearing loss
summary:
Pure-tone and speech audiometry are still among the most important standard tests in ear medicine. They form the foundation for deciding when treatment is needed and for checking how successful it has been.
In 1995, the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS) published guidelines with the goal of making test results easier to compare. This was meant to help create larger data sets for meta-analyses. According to these guidelines, the pure tone average (PTA) is calculated using the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2, and 3 kHz. Since then, these recommendations have been widely discussed and criticized, especially regarding whether these are the right frequencies to use for calculating the PTA. The study includes adults with a pure conductive hearing loss. For patients enrolled prospectively, testing includes pure-tone and speech audiometry as well as a survey on hearing-related quality of life. In addition, adults with conductive hearing loss caused by different conditions are included retrospectively, if pure-tone and speech audiometry results are already available.
conditions: Disorder of middle ear and mastoid, unspecified

interventions.name: Prospective data cohort, pure tone, speech audiometry, quality of life
Retrospective, disease-specific cohorts pure tone and speech audiometry

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
2. an ENT-specialist proven diagnosis of a) otosclerosis, b) acute otitis media (OMA), or c) chronic otitis media (OMC) on one or both ears, 
3. no prior “major” middle ear surgery (except for tympanic paracentesis and tympanostomy tube placements), 
4. existence of both tone and speech audiometry data, 
5. normal bone conduction audiometry (bone conduction better than 30 dB in every tested frequency), and 
6. a conductive hearing loss of 10 dB or more in at least 3 different tested frequencies
Exclusion criteria:
1. minority (age under 18),
2. absence of the aforementioned diagnoses,
3. previous “major” middle ear surgery,
4. absence of pure-tone and/or speech audiometry data,
5. pathological bone conduction audiometry (bone conduction worse than 30 dB in one or more of the tested frequencies), and
6. a conductive hearing loss of 10 dB or more in fewer than three different tested frequencies.
